answer_creator: Domain Expert (Asset-Based Trucking / Freight Margin Recovery)
creation_methodology: Blind review: Expert analyzed public-style carrier disclosures independently. Diagnosed root cause through multi-dimensional evidence (EBITDA margin 11.0%→8.0%, operating ratio 91%→94%, cost-per-mile inflation in fuel +15% and driver wages +12%, revenue-per-mile decline 3.6% to $1.60, flat volumes ~500M miles). Confirmed the break is in per-mile unit economics (unit cost outrunning unit revenue), not demand or a deliberate pricing-structure error.
root_cause_description: The carrier's per-mile unit economics have broken down: cost per mile is rising faster than revenue per mile. Fuel cost per mile rose 15% to $0.40 (+$0.052/mi) and driver wages/benefits per mile rose 12% to $0.62 (+$0.066/mi), together adding ~$0.118/mile of cost on ~500M miles, about +$59M of cost year over year. At the same time revenue per mile fell 3.6% to $1.60 (from $1.66, -$0.06/mi, ~-$30M) because a soft, competitive freight market caps base rates and the fuel surcharge lags the index and under-recovers — especially on the ~30% spot book that carries little surcharge. The net effect is a 300 bps deterioration in operating ratio (91%→94%) and a 300 bps collapse in EBITDA margin (11.0%→8.0%, $87.1M→$64M). Crucially, volumes are roughly flat (revenue $800M vs $792M, ~500M miles), so this is not a demand problem and not a deliberate mispricing of a fixed price list — there is a functioning spot market and rate flexibility. The marginal mile simply no longer covers its incremental cost the way it did, because unit cost outran unit revenue. That is a genuine UNIT_ECONOMICS_BREAKDOWN.

symptoms: EBITDA margin fell 300 bps from 11.0% to 8.0% (EBITDA $87.1M→$64M).
Operating ratio deteriorated from 91% to 94%, nearing the lender covenant threshold.
Owner anxiety about bid season and the annual lender review within ~90 days.
contributing_factors: Fuel cost per mile +15% (to $0.40) with a fuel-surcharge formula that lags the index and does not fully pass through, especially on spot freight.
Driver wages/benefits per mile +12% (to $0.62) driven by a tight CDL labor market and retention needs.
Soft, oversupplied freight market compressing base rates and revenue per mile (-3.6% to $1.60).
Fixed equipment-lease commitments and contract-rate lock-in that prevent fast cost or revenue correction.
symptom_vs_contributing_vs_root_cause.root_cause: Per-mile unit economics have broken: combined cost-per-mile inflation (~+$0.118/mi from fuel and wages) exceeds the revenue-per-mile decline (-$0.06/mi), so contribution per mile has compressed and the operating ratio has risen — a cost-per-unit-of-output vs revenue-per-unit-of-output breakdown, not a volume or list-pricing problem.

first_priority_action: Run a focused cost-per-mile and lane/customer freight-profitability diagnostic (6-week project, ~$60-90k or an internal pricing/FP&A team sprint) to rebuild contribution margin per lane and per customer and pinpoint where the per-mile break is concentrated. Specifically: (1) decompose cost per mile by component (fuel, driver, maintenance, equipment, insurance) and revenue per mile by customer/lane/contract-vs-spot; (2) compute the fuel-surcharge recovery ratio (surcharge collected vs incremental fuel cost) by account to size the under-recovery and identify surcharge re-rate targets at the next bid; (3) rank lanes/customers by contribution per mile to identify the bottom decile that is value-destructive (revenue per mile below loaded cost per mile) for shedding or re-rating at bid season; (4) quantify empty-mile/deadhead percentage, tractor utilization, and driver productivity to find non-rate margin recovery (every point of empty-mile reduction lifts revenue per total mile); (5) build a fleet right-sizing sensitivity (lease roll-off schedule) so the carrier knows how much fixed cost can come out if unprofitable volume is shed. Output: a ranked action set — surcharge re-rate, lane/customer shedding, utilization improvement, and a fleet sizing decision — sequenced to land before bid season and the lender review (~90 days) and to move the operating ratio back off the covenant line.
action_description: This is first priority because the operating ratio is nearing a covenant limit and bid season is ~90 days out, but the carrier cannot act safely without knowing where on the network the per-mile economics break. Cutting driver pay, chasing cheap freight to fill trucks, or slashing maintenance would all be reflexive moves that worsen this specific case. The diagnostic converts a blunt 300-bps margin problem into targeted levers — surcharge re-rate, bottom-decile lane/customer shedding, empty-mile/utilization gains, and a lease-aware fleet sizing decision — that can be committed at the bid table and presented to the lender. At ~6 weeks it fits inside the 90-day window with time left to execute.
accepted_alternative_actions: Fuel-surcharge program re-rating and contract-renewal repricing: rebuild the surcharge formula to track the pump with less lag and extend coverage to as much of the spot/contract book as the market allows, and reprice the lowest-contribution contracts at the next bid cycle. Accepted because it directly attacks the revenue-per-mile-vs-fuel-cost gap without unilaterally raising base rates in a soft market; should be informed by the recovery-ratio diagnostic.

Network/utilization optimization to cut empty miles and raise loaded miles per truck per day: improve load matching, backhaul density, and driver productivity to raise revenue per total mile and spread fixed cost over more loaded miles. Accepted as a parallel non-rate lever that lifts contribution per mile without touching driver pay or shedding strategic customers.
bad_actions: Cut driver wages/benefits to claw back the +12% increase. Wrong for THIS case: the CDL labor market is tight and the raise was made to retain drivers; cutting pay would spike turnover, raise recruiting/training cost, idle trucks, and depress utilization — raising effective cost per mile and worsening the operating ratio, the opposite of the goal.

Chase low-rate freight to keep trucks full. Wrong for THIS case: volumes are already roughly flat and the problem is contribution per mile, not empty trucks. Booking freight at rates below loaded cost per mile (revenue/mile already only $1.60 vs rising cost/mile) adds unprofitable miles and accelerates margin and operating-ratio deterioration.

Defer maintenance to cut the $0.18/mile maintenance line. Wrong for THIS case: deferring maintenance creates DOT/CSA safety and out-of-service risk, raises breakdown and downtime cost, and harms driver retention — trading a small near-term cost reduction for larger safety, compliance, and reliability costs that hit the operating ratio later.

Take on incremental debt or a large capex fleet refresh to 'grow out' of the margin problem. Wrong for THIS case: the operating ratio is nearing a covenant limit ahead of the lender review; adding leverage or fixed cost before fixing per-mile economics increases covenant breach risk and does nothing about the unit-cost-vs-unit-revenue gap.
action_constraints_respected: Competitive spot rates cap pricing: the diagnostic targets surcharge recovery and bottom-decile lane/customer profitability rather than across-the-board rate hikes, so it works within a soft market.
Fuel-surcharge lag: the recovery-ratio analysis is explicitly designed to size and fix surcharge under-recovery at the next bid cycle.
Driver shortage/retention: no action touches driver pay; productivity and utilization levers protect retention.
Equipment lease commitments: fleet right-sizing is modeled against the lease roll-off schedule so only feasible, penalty-aware reductions are proposed.
Customer contracts: rate corrections are sequenced to the bid cycle, not forced mid-term.
Covenant pressure / ~90-day timeline: the 6-week diagnostic and sequenced levers are designed to move the operating ratio before the lender review without large discretionary capital outlays.
rationale: Three diagnoses compete: UNIT_ECONOMICS_BREAKDOWN (cost per mile outran revenue per mile), STRATEGIC_PRICING_ERROR (rates set wrong), and DEMAND_FORECASTING_MISMATCH (volume too low for the cost base). The evidence points to unit economics: volumes and miles are flat (so demand is intact), and the carrier has spot-market and bid-cycle rate flexibility (so this is not a frozen-list mispricing) — yet the operating ratio rose 300 bps because fuel (+$0.052/mi) and driver wages (+$0.066/mi) outran the -$0.06/mi revenue-per-mile decline. The first move is therefore not a blunt cost cut or a rate gamble but a diagnostic that localizes the break (which lanes, which customers, how much surcharge under-recovery, how many empty miles) so surcharge re-rating, lane/customer shedding, utilization gains, and lease-aware fleet sizing can be sequenced before bid season and the lender review.
evidence_basis: financial_health: EBITDA margin 11.0%→8.0% (300 bps, $87.1M→$64M) and operating ratio 91%→94% on essentially flat revenue ($792M→$800M) — costs grew faster than revenue.
operational_efficiency: cost per mile rose via fuel +15% to $0.40 (+$0.052/mi) and driver wages +12% to $0.62 (+$0.066/mi), ~+$0.118/mi and ~+$59M on 500M miles.
market_position: revenue per mile fell 3.6% to $1.60 (from $1.66) in a soft market with lagging, under-recovering fuel surcharge, especially on the ~30% spot book.
operational_efficiency: total miles ~500M and revenue flat confirm stable volume, isolating the break to per-mile contribution (cost-per-mile increase exceeds revenue-per-mile decline).
evidence_not_explained: The split of the revenue-per-mile decline between base-rate erosion and fuel-surcharge under-recovery is not separable from public data; the recovery-ratio diagnostic is required to apportion it. This does not change the UNIT_ECONOMICS_BREAKDOWN diagnosis — both mechanisms compress contribution per mile — but it determines how much can be recovered via surcharge re-rating vs lane shedding.
alternative_explanations: STRATEGIC_PRICING_ERROR: that the carrier simply priced freight wrong. Weaker because there is a functioning spot market and annual bid cycle giving real rate flexibility — the rates are market-driven, not a frozen mispriced list. The -$0.06/mi revenue decline is smaller than the +$0.118/mi cost increase, so the break is driven by unit cost outrunning unit revenue, not by a deliberate pricing-structure mistake. (Distinct from PD-014/PD-018 pricing-structure cases.)

DEMAND_FORECASTING_MISMATCH: that volume fell below the cost base. Weaker because miles (~500M) and revenue ($800M vs $792M) are roughly flat — loads and volumes are stable. The margin broke per mile, not per load count, so there is no demand/capacity mismatch to forecast around.

OPERATIONAL_BOTTLENECK: that a capacity or throughput constraint is the cause. Weaker because trucks are moving freight at stable volume; the issue is the economics of each mile, not a throughput choke point — though empty-mile/utilization improvement is a legitimate secondary lever surfaced by the diagnostic.
missing_evidence: Lane-level and customer-level contribution margin per mile (to identify the value-destructive bottom decile for shedding or re-rating).
Fuel-surcharge recovery ratio by account (surcharge collected vs incremental fuel cost) to size under-recovery and surcharge re-rate targets.
Empty-mile/deadhead percentage and tractor/driver utilization by region (to size non-rate margin recovery).
Equipment lease roll-off schedule and early-termination penalties (to model feasible fleet right-sizing).
success_metrics: Diagnostic complete within 6 weeks: cost per mile decomposed by component and revenue/contribution per mile rebuilt by lane, customer, and contract-vs-spot.
Surcharge under-recovery quantified by account and a re-rate proposal prepared for the next bid cycle.
Bottom-decile (value-destructive) lanes/customers identified with a shed-or-re-rate decision and quantified operating-ratio impact.
Operating ratio improvement path to below ~92% (toward 91%) and EBITDA margin recovery path toward ~10-11% modeled and sequenced to land before the lender review.
Empty-mile / utilization improvement target set (e.g., reduce deadhead by 1-2 points) with quantified revenue-per-total-mile uplift.
expected_outcome: If UNIT_ECONOMICS_BREAKDOWN is correct and the diagnostic is executed well: (1) within 6 weeks, a ranked view of where the per-mile break concentrates (specific lanes/customers, surcharge under-recovery, empty miles); (2) within ~90 days, committed actions at bid season — fuel-surcharge re-rate, bottom-decile lane/customer shedding or repricing, and utilization improvements — that begin moving the operating ratio off the covenant line; (3) a lease-aware fleet right-sizing decision if shed volume warrants it. Combined, these should recover a meaningful share of the 300 bps operating-ratio deterioration and put EBITDA margin on a path back toward 10-11%, with a credible plan to present at the lender review. If the diagnostic instead shows the break is broad and unfixable at current market rates, the carrier must escalate to a larger fleet right-sizing or strategic repositioning rather than incremental fixes.
automatic_fail_conditions: Recommending across-the-board driver pay cuts as the primary fix (spikes turnover in a driver-short market and raises effective cost per mile — directly worsens this case).
Recommending booking low-rate freight below loaded cost per mile to fill trucks (adds unprofitable miles when volume is already stable — accelerates margin and operating-ratio decline).
Recommending deferring maintenance or safety spend to cut cost (creates DOT/CSA and reliability risk that costs more later).
Diagnosing a demand/volume problem or a deliberate list-pricing error despite flat ~500M miles and clear per-mile cost-vs-revenue evidence (misreads the root cause).
Taking on incremental leverage or large capex before fixing per-mile economics, with the operating ratio already near the covenant limit.
source_references: SEC 10-K and operating-statistics supplements for mid-cap truckload/LTL carriers (operating ratio, revenue per mile, cost per mile, fuel surcharge disclosures).
Carrier investor-day operating-statistic supplements (cost-per-mile component breakdown: fuel, driver, maintenance, equipment, insurance).
Industry fuel-surcharge mechanics and freight-rate environment commentary (contract vs spot, surcharge lag and recovery).

required_formulas: Revenue per mile = revenue / total miles
Cost-per-mile inflation contribution = Σ(Δcost component per mile) × total miles
EBITDA margin decline (bps) = (prior EBITDA margin − current EBITDA margin) × 100
Revenue per mile change % = (current revenue per mile − prior revenue per mile) / prior revenue per mile × 100
deterministic_scoring.tolerance: ±0.5 pp on margins and operating ratio; ±$0.01 on per-mile figures; ±5% relative on dollar totals (e.g. cost inflation $59M).
deterministic_scoring.unit_assumptions: Revenue and EBITDA in USD millions. Total miles in millions (500M). Per-mile figures in USD per mile. Margins and operating ratio in percent; bps = percentage points × 100. Cost-per-mile inflation contribution computed on FY2025 total miles (500M). Fuel +15% on $0.348 = $0.40 (+$0.052/mi); wages +12% on $0.554 = $0.62 (+$0.066/mi); combined +$0.118/mi × 500M ≈ $59M. Revenue-per-mile decline -$0.06/mi × 500M ≈ -$30M.
deterministic_scoring.invalid_input_rules: Reject negative miles, negative revenue, EBITDA margin outside 0-100%, operating ratio outside 0-200%, or any per-mile component < 0. Reject if EBITDA margin and operating ratio are mutually inconsistent beyond tolerance (EBITDA margin is pre-D&A and will exceed operating margin; operating ratio uses operating expenses inclusive of D&A). Reject if cost-per-mile components implied total grossly exceeds revenue per mile without explanation.
deterministic_scoring.missing_input_behavior: If a required input for a specific metric is absent, compute only the metrics whose inputs are present and explicitly mark the rest as not computable; do not infer or fabricate inputs.
refuse_if_missing: If total miles is absent, refuse to compute revenue per mile, cost per mile, or cost-per-mile inflation contribution.
If revenue per mile (current or prior) is absent and cannot be derived from revenue/miles, refuse to compute revenue-per-mile change.
If revenue is absent, refuse to compute EBITDA margin and operating ratio.
If per-component cost-per-mile values (or their prior-year values) are absent, refuse to compute the cost-per-mile inflation contribution.

root_cause_accuracy.criterion: Does the engine diagnose UNIT_ECONOMICS_BREAKDOWN, recognizing that per-mile cost (fuel +15%, driver wages +12%) outran per-mile revenue (-3.6% to $1.60) and drove the operating ratio from 91% to 94% and EBITDA margin from 11% to 8%?
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_10: Diagnoses UNIT_ECONOMICS_BREAKDOWN exactly, citing cost-per-mile inflation (fuel +$0.052, wages +$0.066), revenue-per-mile decline to $1.60, operating ratio 91%→94%, and EBITDA 11%→8%, and explicitly notes flat volume rules out demand.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_8: Diagnoses a closely related cost/margin archetype (e.g., OPERATIONAL_BOTTLENECK on cost structure) with sound per-mile reasoning, or UNIT_ECONOMICS_BREAKDOWN without full quantification.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_6: Identifies margin compression and cost-per-mile pressure but does not clearly frame it as a per-mile unit-economics break vs revenue per mile.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_4: Focuses on a secondary issue (general freight-rate weakness or competition) without recognizing the unit-cost-vs-unit-revenue breakdown.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_2: Diagnosis contradicts the evidence (e.g., calls it a demand collapse despite flat 500M miles).
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_0: Diagnosis unrelated to the cost/revenue-per-mile evidence.

first_action_accuracy.criterion: Does the engine recommend a cost-per-mile and lane/customer freight-profitability diagnostic (including fuel-surcharge recovery and utilization) before blunt cost-cutting or rate moves?
first_action_accuracy.rubric_10: Recommends the per-mile / lane-and-customer profitability diagnostic with clear scope (cost-per-mile decomposition, surcharge recovery ratio, bottom-decile lane shedding, empty-mile/utilization, lease-aware fleet sizing), timeline (~6 weeks), and cost, sequenced to bid season and lender review.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_8: Recommends a profitability/cost-structure diagnostic with slightly different scope but still targets per-mile economics before acting.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_6: Recommends investigating costs or profitability but less targeted, or bundles some premature action with the diagnostic.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_4: Recommends immediate cost-cutting (e.g., wage or maintenance cuts) without first localizing the per-mile break.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_2: Recommends aggressive action (mass lane exit, fleet sale, or rate war) without analytical foundation.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_0: Action harmful or contradicts the diagnosis (e.g., chase low-rate freight).

business_relevance.criterion: Does the action reflect asset-based trucking dynamics (operating ratio, revenue per mile, fuel surcharge, driver retention, bid season, covenant review)?
business_relevance.rubric_10: Action is grounded in carrier operating reality — operating ratio toward covenant, revenue/mile, surcharge recovery, empty miles, lease roll-off, bid-cycle repricing — and times levers to the 90-day window.
business_relevance.rubric_6: Relevant to a trucking margin problem but misses one key carrier-specific lever (e.g., surcharge recovery or operating ratio framing).
business_relevance.rubric_2: Generic margin advice that could apply to any industry; ignores per-mile and operating-ratio context.
business_relevance.rubric_0: Irrelevant or harmful to an asset-based carrier.

constraint_awareness.criterion: Does the action respect driver retention (no pay cuts), lease commitments, contract lock-in, the ~90-day timeline, and covenant pressure?
constraint_awareness.rubric_10: Action protects driver pay, models fleet sizing against lease roll-off, sequences rate fixes to the bid cycle, fits ~6 weeks inside the 90-day window, and avoids new leverage near the covenant limit.
constraint_awareness.rubric_6: Respects most constraints with minor tension (e.g., timeline or cost slightly aggressive).
constraint_awareness.rubric_2: Violates a hard constraint (e.g., cuts driver pay or assumes mid-term contract repricing).

evidence_traceability.criterion: Can every diagnosis/action claim be traced to the case financials?
evidence_traceability.rubric_10: All key claims traced: EBITDA 11%→8% ($87.1M→$64M), operating ratio 91%→94%, revenue/mile $1.66→$1.60 (-3.6%), fuel $0.40 (+15%/+$0.052), wages $0.62 (+12%/+$0.066), ~500M miles, ~$59M cost inflation.
evidence_traceability.rubric_6: Main diagnosis supported; some claims not tied to specific figures.

confidence_calibration.criterion: Is HIGH confidence appropriate given the evidence?
confidence_calibration.rubric_10: HIGH well-calibrated: audited-style multi-year financials, clear per-mile cost and revenue trends, and flat volume jointly pin the diagnosis; residual unknowns (lane-level splits) do not threaten it.
confidence_calibration.rubric_6: Evidence supports the diagnosis but lane-level/surcharge detail missing; MODERATE-to-HIGH might be defended.
confidence_calibration.rubric_2: Evidence ambiguous or weak for the stated confidence.

safety.criterion: Is the action safe (diagnostic before blunt cost-cutting; protects driver retention, safety/maintenance, and covenant position)?
safety.rubric_10: Low-risk diagnostic that localizes the break before irreversible moves; explicitly avoids pay cuts, maintenance deferral, low-rate freight, and new leverage near covenant.
safety.rubric_6: Mostly safe but with one underweighted risk (e.g., light on maintenance/safety or covenant framing).
safety.rubric_2: Recommends a risky move (aggressive cost-cut or rate war) with weak safeguards.
safety.rubric_0: Unsafe: pay cuts, maintenance deferral, low-rate freight, or new leverage that worsens this case.
